summary: First English narrative for the October 1873 reversal of the Saigo envoy decision, written from the case's structured facts.

narrative.hook: Two months ago your government decided to send an envoy to Korea, and the Emperor signed off on it. Now your most senior colleagues are back from eighteen months abroad, and they are telling you the country cannot afford whatever this starts. Undoing it means overruling the Emperor's own approval and breaking the most admired man in Japan.
narrative.short_setup: It is October 1873, less than six years after the Meiji Restoration. Korea's Joseon court, under the Daewongun's regency, has repeatedly refused to accept Japanese diplomatic letters written in the new imperial terminology, and Japanese officials report insulting notices posted at Busan. In August the Council of State approved Saigo Takamori's proposal to go to Korea himself as special envoy — a proposal he argued for partly on the ground that if Korea killed him, Japan would have unambiguous cause for a punitive expedition. The Emperor assented on August 17-18. Then Okubo Toshimichi, Iwakura Tomomi and the rest of the Iwakura Mission came home from a year and a half touring the industrial and military powers of the United States and Europe. Chancellor Sanjo Sanetomi has fallen ill. Iwakura holds his authority.
narrative.why_option_a_made_sense: To the officials who had stayed in Japan, the case for going ahead was not bravado. Korea's refusal to deal with the new imperial court was an unresolved standing rebuff, and there was no reason to think waiting would soften it — delay might instead let Korea strengthen its own position or draw closer to Qing China or Russia, both of which had interests on the peninsula. The Restoration's unity and momentum were an asset with a shelf life. And there was a domestic problem pressing at the same time: a large samurai class had just lost its stipends and its social role, and some contemporaries saw a national mission abroad as an answer to that strain. Against all this, Saigo's willingness to stake his own life read, to his supporters, as seriousness rather than recklessness.
narrative.why_option_b_made_sense: Okubo and Iwakura had an argument nobody in Tokyo could have made two years earlier, because they had just been to see for themselves. Eighteen months among Western factories, shipyards and armies had given them a concrete sense of the gap, and Okubo's written opinion — his '7 Points Document' — said plainly that action against Korea was premature and that a war would cost more than Japan could bear at this stage. This was not general caution. It was a specific comparative judgment by people who had just done the comparison. And the programme they wanted the money and attention for — land tax reform, conscription, industrial development — was the thing that would eventually make any such confrontation survivable.
narrative.actual_decision_explanation: Iwakura, holding acting authority over the Council of State while Sanjo was ill, took Okubo's case to Emperor Meiji, and the August approval was reversed around October 22-23, 1873. The stated basis was Okubo's: the action was premature given Japan's unfinished modernisation, and the cost of a war was more than the state could carry. The institutional fact underneath is worth naming plainly — this was the reversal of a decision the Emperor had formally approved two months earlier, carried out by a faction that had been out of the country when it was made.
narrative.outcome_story: Saigo resigned as Councillor of State and commander of the Imperial Guard on October 23. Itagaki Taisuke, Goto Shojiro, Eto Shimpei and Soejima Taneomi resigned the next day, accepted on October 25; more than a hundred Imperial Guard officers loyal to Saigo left with them. On the external question the reversal held: Japan mounted no major campaign against Korea in the 1870s, and instead used a limited naval incident at Ganghwa Island in 1875 to force the Treaty of Ganghwa in 1876, opening Korean ports without the general war Saigo's mission risked. Domestically the bill came due elsewhere. Eto Shimpei led the Saga Rebellion in 1874. Saigo went home to Satsuma and founded private military academies for former samurai; those academies became the base of the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877, the largest armed uprising the Meiji government ever faced, in which tens of thousands were killed or wounded and Saigo died.
narrative.hindsight_analysis: Hold two things apart here, because the case makes it tempting to collapse them. The judgment that Japan could not sustain a war in 1873 looks sound, and it looks sound on grounds available in 1873: it rested on recent, firsthand, comparative observation rather than temperament, and the people making it had just spent eighteen months acquiring exactly the information the question needed. That is a good reason to believe something. What keeps the decision short of strong is not the conclusion but what came attached to it. Reversing an imperial approval two months old, against the most prominent figure in the government, carried political costs that were foreseeable at the time — not the Satsuma Rebellion specifically, but the fracture of the governing coalition and the departure of Saigo with his following intact. And the reversal answered the Korea question only by deferring it; no alternative resolution was offered. The outcome then split. On the international question it was vindicated, though partly by a route nobody had proposed in the debate: the 1876 treaty came through gunboat coercion at a moment of Japan's choosing, not through patience alone. Domestically it was not vindicated at all, and the 1877 rebellion is a real cost of this decision, even though it took four years, other people's choices, and Saigo's own subsequent actions to arrive. Calling it caused by the reversal overstates it; calling it unrelated understates it. It is what happens when you win an argument about capacity and lose the man who commanded the loyalty.
narrative.decision_principle: Being right about the substance does not settle what a reversal costs. When you overturn a decision that has already been made and blessed, the price of the reversal is a separate question from the merits — and it has to be paid by someone.
narrative.longform_story:
In the autumn of 1873 the Japanese government came apart over a question it never actually answered.

The proximate issue was Korea. The Joseon court, under the regency of the Daewongun, had for several years refused to accept diplomatic communications from Japan that used the terminology of the new Meiji imperial order — a refusal that was, from Tokyo's side, a denial of the new state's standing. Japanese officials reported insulting notices posted at Busan. The rebuff was real, it was repeated, and it had no obvious end.

In August 1873 the Council of State took it up. Saigo Takamori — Councillor of State, commander of the Imperial Guard, and the closest thing the Restoration had to a popular hero — proposed going to Korea himself as a special envoy. Multiple accounts record him arguing, in the Council, that if Korea killed him, Japan would then have clear and unambiguous grounds for a punitive expedition. The Council approved. The Emperor assented on August 17 and 18.

What happened next was not a change of facts but a change of who was in the room.

For the previous year and a half, a substantial part of the Meiji leadership had been abroad. The Iwakura Mission — Iwakura Tomomi, Okubo Toshimichi, Kido Takayoshi and others — had spent eighteen months touring the United States and the industrial powers of Europe. They came back with something the officials who had stayed behind did not have: a direct, physical, recent sense of the scale of what Japan was measuring itself against. Factories. Shipyards. Standing armies.

Okubo wrote an opinion against the Korea proposal — the document usually referred to as his seven points. Its argument was not that the grievance was imaginary or that the honour of the state did not matter. It was that the action was premature, that Japan's modernisation was in its early stages, and that a war would cost more than the country could currently sustain.

This is worth pausing on, because it is the part that makes the case interesting rather than obvious. Okubo's position was not general prudence. Anyone can counsel patience. What he had was a specific comparative judgment formed by having just done the comparison — the closest thing available in 1873 to evidence about the question actually at hand.

The other side was not empty either. To officials who had remained in Japan, the argument for acting now had its own logic. The rebuff from Korea was live and might worsen. Delay could allow Korea to consolidate, or to draw closer to Qing China or Russia, both with interests on the peninsula. The unity that the Restoration had generated was an asset that would not last forever. And there was a domestic pressure running underneath: the samurai class had recently lost its stipends and its function, and some contemporaries — and some later historians — held that a national mission abroad was seen, by parts of that class and by supporters like Itagaki Taisuke, as an answer to that displacement. Whether that was the real driver is a question the sources do not settle; it is a belief about motive, not a documented motive.

So is Saigo's own intent. The traditional account, and Britannica's summary, has him deliberately courting assassination to manufacture a pretext. More recent biographical scholarship, notably Mark Ravina's, argues that this framing partly reflects Saigo's rhetorical positioning inside the Council debate — aimed in part at bringing Itagaki along — and that his actual aim may have been closer to establishing direct, formal relations with Korea than to provoking a war. What is documented is what he said. What he meant by it remains contested, and this account does not pretend otherwise.

The mechanism of the reversal mattered as much as its substance. Chancellor Sanjo Sanetomi fell ill, and Iwakura took over his authority as acting head of the Council of State. That gave him standing to bring the matter directly before the Emperor. He did, carrying Okubo's argument, and around October 22-23 the August approval was undone.

Saigo resigned on October 23. Itagaki, Goto Shojiro, Eto Shimpei and Soejima Taneomi resigned the following day; the resignations were accepted on the 25th. More than a hundred Imperial Guard officers loyal to Saigo left government service with him. The coalition that had made the Restoration had split, in a week, over a mission that never sailed.

On the question the debate was nominally about, the reversal held and looks well-judged. Japan mounted no major campaign against Korea in the 1870s. When it did force the issue, it did so by a narrower route than anything proposed in 1873: a limited naval incident at Ganghwa Island in 1875, followed by the Treaty of Ganghwa in 1876, which opened Korean ports under coercion but without general war. Meanwhile the internal programme proceeded — land tax reform, conscription, industrial development — which was what Okubo had wanted the time and money for.

The domestic reckoning came separately, and it came hard. Eto Shimpei, one of the men who resigned in October 1873, led the Saga Rebellion in 1874. Saigo returned to Satsuma and established private military academies for former samurai. Those academies became the organisational and manpower base of the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877: the largest and most serious armed uprising the Meiji government ever faced, ending in tens of thousands killed or wounded, the definitive supremacy of the new conscript army over the old samurai class, and Saigo's own death.

How should the decision be scored? Carefully, and in two pieces.

The conclusion — that Japan could not sustain a war in 1873 — was well-grounded, and its grounding was visible at the time. That is what good reasoning under uncertainty looks like: not certainty, but the best available evidence actually applied to the question.

What the decision did not do was price the reversal. Undoing an imperial approval two months old, over the objection of the most prominent man in the government, had costs that were foreseeable in October 1873 — not the specific shape of 1877, but the fracture of the leadership and the departure of Saigo with his following intact and his prestige undiminished. Nor did the reversal propose any resolution to the underlying standoff with Korea. It deferred.

And the outcome does not cleanly settle the argument either way. Internationally it looks vindicated, though partly through a path nobody in the Council had advocated. Domestically it does not. Blaming the Satsuma Rebellion on the reversal overstates the chain — four years passed, and many other people's choices, including Saigo's own, fill the gap. Calling it unrelated understates it just as badly.

What the case leaves is a narrower lesson, and a durable one. The faction that was right about capacity was also the faction that had been out of the country, and it won by procedural advantage at a moment of illness and absence. Being right about the substance told them nothing about what the reversal would cost, or who would end up paying it.
